title: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
summary: How unikernels link an application with only the OS libraries it needs into one image that boots on a hypervisor, why that removes syscall costs, and what it costs in security, compatibility and tooling.
outcomes: Explain why a single-application VM does not need a user/kernel split and what isolation the hypervisor provides instead
Compute the speedup from turning syscalls into function calls for a given request profile
Describe how micro-libraries, static linking and dead code elimination produce a small specialized image
Explain where unikernel boot time goes and why the VMM dominates it
Decide when a unikernel fits a service, weighing security, compatibility, debugging and porting costs

lessons.title: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant

blocks.md:
A typical cloud server is one application, say a DNS server or nginx, inside a virtual machine (VM). The VM boots a full general-purpose OS: a kernel, a C library, a shell, cron, package tooling, and the application. The hypervisor (the software that splits one physical machine into many VMs, like Xen or KVM) already isolates this VM from every other tenant.

Inside the VM, the guest kernel then isolates the application from... nothing else. There is only one application. Yet every read, write and send still crosses the user/kernel boundary you met in the system calls course, paying a mode switch each time.

A **unikernel** removes that inner layer. Madhavapeddy and colleagues coined the term in their 2013 ASPLOS paper: a *specialised, sealed, single-purpose library OS VM that runs directly on the hypervisor*.

A **library operating system** (libOS) implements OS services such as the scheduler, device drivers and network stack as ordinary libraries linked into the application. The compiler and linker then produce **one bootable image** that contains the application plus only the OS code it uses, in **one address space** and at **one privilege level**.

blocks.title: The same server as a classic VM and as a unikernel

scenes.caption: A classic VM appliance: the application sits on a full guest OS, which sits on the hypervisor. Most of the user space is never used by nginx.
Two isolation mechanisms are stacked. The hypervisor separates tenants; the guest kernel separates user from kernel inside a VM that holds only one application.
Every send or read pays a trap from user mode into the guest kernel, then the kernel talks to the virtual device.
The unikernel keeps the hypervisor as its only isolation boundary. The OS services become libraries linked next to the application.
Its request path has no trap: a socket call is a plain function call into the network library, which drives the same virtual device.

blocks.md:
Library OSes are an old idea: Exokernel (1995) and Nemesis (1996) put OS services into application libraries. They never caught on, the Mirage paper argues, because a libOS had to ship drivers for real, endlessly varied hardware.

The hypervisor removes that problem. It presents a small, stable set of **virtual devices** (Xen's netfront and blkfront, or virtio on KVM), so a unikernel needs only a handful of simple drivers. The cloud turned the libOS from a research toy into something you can deploy.

What does dropping the general-purpose OS buy? The Mirage DNS appliance compiled to a VM image of **183.5 kB**, while the in-use Linux VM image for BIND was **462 MB**, about 2,500 times larger. Part of the gap is features (Mirage's DNS server implements less than BIND); much of the rest is code a DNS server never needs: shells, package managers, drivers for hardware the VM will never see.

The Unikraft paper (EuroSys 2021) reports the same pattern for mainstream software: nginx, SQLite and Redis images of around 1 MB that run in under 10 MB of RAM.
A unikernel is **one application plus only the OS code it uses, linked into one image that boots directly on a hypervisor**. The hypervisor, not a guest kernel, is the isolation boundary.

A unikernel is not a container. A container shares the host's Linux kernel and is isolated by kernel features (namespaces, cgroups). A unikernel is a real VM with its own tiny kernel, isolated by hardware virtualization.

blocks.question: A team runs exactly one Redis process per VM on a multi-tenant cloud. Which protection does the guest kernel's user/kernel split still provide that the hypervisor does not?
options: It stops other tenants from reading Redis's memory
It is required for the VM to reach the network card
It protects the guest kernel's code and data from a bug or exploit in Redis, inside that one VM
It prevents Redis from being slowed by noisy neighbours
blocks.explain: Tenant isolation and device access come from the hypervisor. The only thing the inner split still buys is protecting the guest kernel from the single application. In a unikernel, a compromised application owns the whole VM, but the VM is all it can reach; this tradeoff comes back in the last lesson.

blocks.question: Why did library operating systems from the 1990s, such as Exokernel, never see wide deployment, while unikernels can run on public clouds?
options: Their libraries were written in unsafe languages
They had to support many kinds of real hardware; a hypervisor exposes a few standard virtual devices instead
They required multicore CPUs that did not exist yet
Hypervisors run library OSes faster than bare metal does
blocks.explain: The Mirage paper's argument: libOSes struggled with real-world hardware support. A hypervisor's virtual devices (netfront, blkfront, virtio) are a small, stable target, so only a few simple drivers are needed.

lessons.title: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level

blocks.md:
Recall from the system calls course: a syscall makes the CPU switch from user mode to kernel mode, run kernel entry code and switch back. With KPTI (kernel page-table isolation, the Meltdown mitigation) it also swaps page tables on every entry and exit.

A unikernel has **no user mode at all** for its application. The application, libc and OS libraries share one address space and run at one privilege level, so what used to be a syscall can be an ordinary call instruction.

The Unikraft authors measured a no-op call on an Intel i7-9700K at 3.6 GHz running Linux 5.11 (Table 1 of the paper):

- Linux/KVM syscall: **222 cycles** (61.67 ns)
- Linux/KVM syscall, mitigations off: **154 cycles** (42.78 ns)
- Unikraft/KVM syscall through run-time translation: **84 cycles** (23.33 ns)
- A plain function call, on either: **4 cycles** (1.11 ns)

The third row is Unikraft's *binary compatibility* path: an unmodified Linux binary still executes `syscall`, and Unikraft catches and translates it. That is 2.64 times cheaper than Linux with mitigations, but still 21 times the cost of a function call.

blocks.title: Cost of one no-op call (cycles, i7-9700K)

scenes.caption: Linux with its default security mitigations: 222 cycles to enter and leave the kernel for a call that does nothing.
Turning mitigations such as KPTI off saves 68 cycles, but the mode switch itself remains: 154 cycles.
A unikernel running an unmodified binary must still catch each syscall instruction: 84 cycles, cheaper because there is no real privilege change to make.
When the application is linked against the OS libraries, the syscall is a function call: 4 cycles. This is the number unikernels are built to reach.

blocks.md:
How does an unmodified C program end up making function calls? Unikraft ports the **musl** C library and adds a **syscall shim** micro-library. Each OS library registers its handlers with a macro, `UK_SYSCALL_R_DEFINE`, and the shim generates the libc-level system call interface from them.

Build the application with its own build system, link the object files into the Unikraft image, and every `write` or `recvmsg` in the program resolves at link time to the handler function. The paper calls this **automatic porting**.

blocks.title: Following one write() through each design

scenes.caption: The application code is the same in both worlds. It calls write with file descriptor 1 and a 3 byte buffer.
On Linux, libc loads the syscall number and executes the syscall instruction: a mode switch, entry code and possibly a page table swap. About 222 cycles before any real work.
In Unikraft the shim macro turns the handler into an ordinary C function named after the syscall. The call from libc is a direct jump.
The handler looks up the descriptor in the file descriptor table, the same job the Linux kernel does, but without leaving the address space.
It writes through the open file object and returns the byte count straight to the caller. Simplified: real handlers also take locks when threads are enabled.

blocks.md: How much does this matter for a real server? Model one request as $w$ microseconds of application work plus $k$ syscalls. Only the crossing cost changes between the two designs, so the speedup is:

blocks.tex: S = \frac{w + k \cdot t_{\text{sys}}}{w + k \cdot t_{\text{call}}}, \qquad t_{\text{sys}} = 61.67\,\text{ns},\; t_{\text{call}} = 1.11\,\text{ns}
blocks.caption: With w = 5 microseconds and k = 10 syscalls: (5000 + 616.7) / (5000 + 11.1) = 1.12, a 12% gain. With w = 1 microsecond the same 10 syscalls give 1.60.

blocks.title: Speedup from removing the syscall crossing

curves.label: Linux no mitigations vs function call

scenes.caption: With 10 syscalls per request, a 5 microsecond request speeds up 1.12 times and a 1 microsecond request 1.60 times. Simplified: counts only the crossing, not cache or TLB effects.
With 50 syscalls and 0.1 microseconds of work, the request is almost all crossing: speedup 20.5. Tiny, I/O-heavy requests gain the most.
With 1 syscall per request the curve is nearly flat: at 10 microseconds of work the gain is 0.6%. Compute-bound code gains almost nothing.

blocks.prompt: Unikraft compared nginx and Redis on Unikraft (in a KVM VM) against the same programs running natively on bare-metal Linux, with no hypervisor at all. Which do you expect was faster?
blocks.reveal: Unikraft was **10% to 60% faster than native Linux** in both applications, and 70% to 170% faster than a Linux VM. The authors attribute this to syscall cost (worse with KPTI on) and to linking the mimalloc allocator into the image. A VM is not automatically slower than bare metal when the OS inside it does less work per request.

blocks.md: Unikernel speed comes from **removing the user/kernel crossing**, not from a faster CPU path. Gains are largest for small, syscall-heavy requests and near zero for compute-bound code.

Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

blocks.question: A request handler spends 50 microseconds computing and makes 10 syscalls. Using the model above, roughly how much faster does it get on a unikernel?
options: About 1%
About 12%
About 60%
About 2.6 times
blocks.explain: S = (50000 + 616.7) / (50000 + 11.1) = 1.012, about 1.2%. Removing 600 ns of crossings barely matters next to 50 microseconds of compute.

blocks.question: A team runs an unmodified Linux nginx binary on a unikernel through its binary compatibility layer and sees less gain than the papers report. What is the most likely reason?
options: Binary compatibility disables the hypervisor's virtio drivers
nginx needs fork, which unikernels emulate with slow VM cloning
The binary is compiled for user mode and cannot run in kernel mode
Each syscall instruction still has to be trapped and translated, which costs far more than a direct function call
blocks.explain: The unmodified binary still executes syscall instructions, which the unikernel must catch and dispatch: 84 cycles versus 4 for a direct call in Unikraft's measurement. Linking the application against musl and the syscall shim turns those into direct calls.

lessons.title: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code

blocks.md:
A unikernel is specialized **at build time**. Instead of shipping a general OS and configuring it at run time, you pick the OS components your application needs, compile them together with it, and let the compiler and linker throw away everything else.

Unikraft makes this explicit. Every OS component is a **micro-library**: a scheduler, a memory allocator, a network stack, a virtio driver, the boot code. Each has its own Makefile and Kconfig file (the same configuration menu system Linux uses). The build system compiles the selected micro-libraries and links them into one image per target platform.

Micro-libraries that implement the same **API** are interchangeable. Five allocators implement `ukalloc`; cooperative and preemptive schedulers implement `uksched`; lwip and others sit on `uknetdev`. An application can also skip a layer entirely: a run-to-completion server can leave the scheduler out, and a packet processor can call the network driver API without any TCP/IP stack.

blocks.title: Which micro-libraries end up in the image

scenes.caption: The menu of micro-libraries. Nothing is in the image until the configuration or a dependency pulls it in.
Hello world: only platform boot code and nolibc (a tiny Unikraft libc with memcpy and string functions); not even a scheduler or an allocator. The paper reports 200 KB on KVM and 40 KB on Xen.
nginx adds musl, the syscall shim, sockets, a RAM filesystem, a scheduler and the lwip network stack. No block device layer: it only uses ramfs.
A specialized UDP packet server drops the socket layer, lwip and the scheduler, and calls the uknetdev driver API directly in a polling loop.

blocks.md:
Static linking is what makes removal automatic. With every component compiled into one binary, the linker sees the whole program, so **dead code elimination** (DCE: dropping functions and sections nothing references) and **link-time optimization** (LTO: optimizing across what used to be separate libraries) work across the application and the OS together.

Mirage showed the effect in 2013. Its default OCaml build drops unused modules; a dataflow tool called ocamlclean then also drops unused functions inside modules.

blocks.title: Mirage appliance image sizes before and after DCE (MB)

scenes.caption: Standard builds, which already drop unused modules: 0.39 to 0.67 MB including configuration and data.
After function-level dead code elimination: 57% to 74% smaller. The web server shrinks most, from 0.673 to 0.172 MB, 3.9 times smaller.

blocks.md: Configuration moves into the build as well. Mirage compiles configuration files and even data (such as a DNS zone) into the image. That turns misconfiguration into a compile error and lets dead code elimination remove unused features, but it has a cost: to change a setting you rebuild and redeploy. The Mirage paper notes that statically configured VMs can no longer be cloned from one snapshot, and suggests dynamic directives (DHCP instead of a fixed IP) where cloning matters.

blocks.caption: Unikraft's ukalloc front end (lib/ukalloc/include/uk/alloc.h). It is inline, so choosing a backend adds no extra call.

blocks.md: Swapping a component is a configuration change, and the choice matters. With nginx, guest boot time ranged from **0.49 ms with bootalloc** (a simple region allocator) to **3.07 ms with the buddy allocator**, 6.3 times longer. For Redis, the right allocator raised throughput by up to 2.5 times. No single allocator won every workload.

blocks.prompt: For SQLite, Unikraft tried autoporting: build SQLite with its own build system and link the static library into the image, with no source changes. How much slower do you expect it to be than a hand-ported version?
blocks.reveal: Only **1.5% slower** than the manually ported version for 60,000 inserts, and slightly faster than Linux on bare metal. Linking a normal static library into the image already removes the syscall crossings; hand porting adds little on top.

blocks.md: Build-time specialization = **pick components by configuration, link statically, let DCE and LTO remove the rest**. Reconfiguring means rebuilding.

blocks.question: A unikernel serves files only from a RAM filesystem. Why does its image contain no block device driver, even though the Unikraft source tree has one?
options: The hypervisor provides block storage, so the driver is never needed
Block drivers are loaded as kernel modules at boot
Only components selected in the configuration or pulled in as dependencies are compiled and linked; nothing references the block layer
Dead code elimination removes all drivers by default
blocks.explain: Unikraft builds only selected micro-libraries and their dependencies. The paper notes the nginx image has no block subsystem because it only uses RamFS. There are no loadable modules in a unikernel.

blocks.question: A function-as-a-service platform boots a fresh nginx unikernel for each burst of requests and destroys it after a few seconds. Which allocator choice from the Unikraft measurements fits best?
options: A fast-booting allocator such as bootalloc, because boot time dominates a short-lived instance
The buddy allocator, because its throughput at steady state matched TLSF and mimalloc
Any allocator, because allocator choice only affects throughput
mimalloc, because it is always fastest
blocks.explain: For just-in-time instances, boot time matters most, and allocator choice moved nginx guest boot from 0.49 ms (bootalloc) to 3.07 ms (buddy). The paper itself says such a use case should avoid the buddy allocator.

lessons.title: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory

blocks.md:
A unikernel boots as a normal VM. A **virtual machine monitor** (VMM: the user-space program that creates the VM, such as QEMU or Firecracker on KVM) loads the image into guest memory and starts the virtual CPU at its entry point. From there the unikernel's own boot code sets up memory and drivers and calls the application's `main`.

There is no init system, no root filesystem to mount, no services to start. The boot path does only what the selected libraries need.

blocks.title: From VMM start to the first request

scenes.caption: The VMM creates the VM, copies the image into guest memory and starts the virtual CPU at the image's entry point.
Unikraft's default image carries a pre-built page table. Boot code just enables paging and points the CPU at it: about 30 microseconds for 1 GB of memory.
The boot code hands the heap to the configured allocator, then initializes only the drivers in the image, such as virtio-net.
Then it calls main. The guest part of boot, from first instruction to main, took tens to hundreds of microseconds on QEMU and Solo5.
From now on, a send is a function call into the network library, which places the packet on the virtio ring and notifies the host.

blocks.md:
The device interface a unikernel needs is small. Solo5, the sandboxed execution environment that runs MirageOS on KVM and other hosts, exposes a small guest API: acquire, read and write for a network device and for a block device, a monotonic and a wall clock, a console write, `solo5_yield` to sleep until I/O is ready or a deadline passes, thread-local storage setup, and exit. Everything above that (TCP/IP, filesystems, TLS) is library code inside the unikernel.

On Xen, Mirage's drivers speak the split-driver protocol: a shared memory page of request slots with producer and consumer indices, plus an event channel to signal the other side.

Because the guest does so little, **the VMM dominates boot time**. For a hello world on Unikraft, total boot (VMM plus guest) was about 3 ms on Firecracker and Solo5, about 10 ms with QEMU's microVM machine type and about 40 ms with standard QEMU. The guest's own share was under 1 ms in every case.

blocks.title: Where boot time goes (hello world on Unikraft)

scenes.caption: Lightweight VMMs set up a VM in a few milliseconds. The guest share (green) is at most 1 ms. Simplified: totals rounded from the paper, guest shares are upper bounds.
Heavier VMMs emulate more devices and firmware. QEMU microVM reaches about 10 ms and standard QEMU about 40 ms, with the same tiny guest share.
The lesson: once the guest is a unikernel, shaving the guest further barely moves total boot. Pick a lightweight VMM.

blocks.md: Guest boot time is where the OS design shows. The Unikraft paper lists guest boot times reported for other systems: MirageOS 1 to 2 ms on Solo5, OSv 4 to 5 ms on Firecracker, Rump 14 to 15 ms on Solo5, HermiTux 30 to 32 ms on uHyve, Lupine (a specialized Linux) 70 ms on Firecracker, and an Alpine Linux VM about 330 ms on Firecracker.

blocks.title: Guest boot time by OS (upper end of reported range, ms)

scenes.caption: A general-purpose Linux guest takes about 330 ms to boot. Every specialized system is at least 4.7 times faster.
Among unikernels, the ones that initialize least boot fastest: Unikraft under 1 ms and MirageOS 2 ms. Rough comparison only: the VMMs differ.

blocks.md: Memory follows the same logic. Unikraft guests needed only **2 to 6 MB** of RAM to boot nginx, Redis, SQLite or hello world. Mirage's web appliance ran in 32 MB against 256 MB for the Linux VM it was compared with. Small footprints mean more VMs per host, and fast boots mean VMs can be started per request instead of kept warm.

blocks.title: Mirage's sealing: no page writable and executable

scenes.caption: At start of day, before sealing, nothing stops a page from being both writable and executable.
The unikernel builds page tables in which code is read and execute only and every writable page is non-executable (W xor X).
It then issues a seal hypercall. The hypervisor refuses later page table changes, so injected code can never become executable. I/O mappings stay allowed if non-executable.
An exploit that writes code into the heap and tries to mark it executable fails: the hypervisor rejects the page table change. The cost is a fixed heap size from boot.

blocks.md: Mirage also randomizes addresses **at compile time**: since reconfiguring means relinking anyway, each build can use a freshly generated linker script, instead of shipping a runtime loader for address space layout randomization. Sealing needed a hypervisor patch of under 50 lines to Xen 4.1; without it Mirage still runs, minus that defence.

Do not assume every unikernel does this. Sealing and compile-time randomization are Mirage's design; a 2019 NCC Group study of Rumprun and IncludeOS found ASLR, W xor X and stack canaries absent or broken.

blocks.question: A unikernel's guest boot takes 0.3 ms and total VM start takes 40 ms on standard QEMU. What will most reduce cold-start latency?
options: Removing more micro-libraries from the image
Using a faster memory allocator
Moving from KVM to emulation mode
Switching to a lightweight VMM such as Firecracker or Solo5
blocks.explain: The guest is under 1% of the 40 ms. Unikraft's measurements put total boot at about 3 ms on Firecracker and Solo5 versus about 40 ms on QEMU, so the VMM choice is the lever.

blocks.question: Mirage seals a unikernel so no page table changes are allowed after start of day. Which consequence must the application live with?
options: It cannot receive network packets
It must pre-allocate all the memory it needs at startup, since the heap cannot grow by mapping new pages
It cannot use a garbage collector
It must run with a single vCPU
blocks.explain: The paper states a sealed VM cannot expand its heap and must pre-allocate its memory at boot; allocation within the heap and I/O mappings still work. The single vCPU in Mirage is a separate design choice, not a consequence of sealing.

lessons.title: Specializing further, and what you give up

blocks.md:
Removing syscalls helps unmodified applications. The bigger wins come when an application is **rewritten against lower-level APIs** that a general-purpose OS cannot expose without breaking its own layering.

The Unikraft authors built a UDP key-value store, one request per packet, and ran it several ways. The basic version uses `recvmsg` and `sendmsg`, one packet per call. Batching (`recvmmsg`/`sendmmsg`) amortizes the syscalls. Porting to DPDK (a kernel bypass framework: the application polls the network card directly from user space) removes the kernel from the data path entirely.

scenes.caption: Socket APIs everywhere: one syscall per packet. Batching adds about 50% (418 to 627 K/s in the guest), but all of these stay near a million or below.
Note the Unikraft lwip version: 319 K/s, below the Linux guest. Removing syscalls does not help if the network stack itself is slower.
Coding against the driver API changes the scale: DPDK in a Linux guest reaches 6.4 M/s and Unikraft's uknetdev in polling mode 6.3 M/s, 19.7 times its lwip version.

blocks.md: Throughput alone says the two fast versions tie. The resources differ: the DPDK guest used **two cores** (one dedicated to DPDK), about 1 GB of image and a boot of a few seconds. The Unikraft version used **one core**, a 1.4 MB image and booted in 80 ms. Per core, that is 3.2 versus 6.3 million requests per second. Both needed a similar porting effort, since both mean rewriting the network path.

blocks.prompt: Given those numbers, would you expect a Unikraft image running unmodified nginx with its lwip stack to beat Linux on raw packet processing in general?
blocks.reveal: Not necessarily. The key-value store showed lwip on Unikraft at 319 K/s, **below** the Linux guest's 418 K/s with sockets. The nginx and Redis gains came from syscall savings and allocator choice, not a faster TCP/IP stack. Linux's network stack is heavily tuned; a unikernel's stack may not be. Measure your workload.

blocks.md:
Now the costs. The papers and later studies agree on four.

1. **Security hardening may be missing.** The NCC Group study (2019) found ASLR, W xor X, stack canaries and heap integrity checks absent or flawed in Rumprun and IncludeOS. Worse, with no privilege split, code execution in the application *is* code execution in the kernel: an attacker can immediately do things like arbitrary packet I/O that would need privilege escalation on Linux.
2. **Compatibility is partial.** Unikraft's docs report 160+ Linux syscalls implemented; missing ones are stubbed and return ENOSYS. Everything shares one address space, so a copying `fork` is impossible. The 2021 paper supported no processes at all; current Unikraft adds optional `vfork` and `execve` (posix-process), but software built around `fork` still needs a thread-based mode or changes.

3. **Debugging and operations change.** There is no shell to log into, no `ps`, no `strace` inside the VM. Unikraft offers gdb support, a ukdebug library with trace points, and a `linuxu` target that builds the same image as a Linux user-space program for development. Mirage similarly develops on a Unix target first and builds for Xen last.
4. **Scaling is per VM.** Mirage runs one vCPU per unikernel and scales by running more unikernels; Unikraft's paper evaluated single-core images and listed multi-core support as work in progress. Check the current project docs before assuming SMP.

blocks.title: Choosing a deployment model for one service

nodes.label:
Need many processes,
fork, or a shell?

Cold start, density or
attack surface matter?

Hot path needs more
than syscall savings?

scenes.caption: First filter: unikernels have one process. Software built around fork, many cooperating processes or interactive shells belongs in a Linux VM or container.
If nothing pushes you to millisecond boots, high density or a minimal attack surface, a container gives most of the convenience with familiar tools.
Otherwise link the application into a unikernel. If the hot path is bound by the stack itself, rewrite it against the low-level API, as with the key-value store.

blocks.md: Unikernels trade **generality for specialization**: fewer layers, smaller images, faster boots and cheaper calls, paid for with porting work, partial POSIX, no processes, weaker tooling and security that depends entirely on what the libOS implements.

MirageOS's answer to the security cost is language safety: its whole stack, TCP/IP included, is OCaml. The paper notes that of 40 BIND vulnerabilities over 10 years, 25% were memory management errors, 15% poor handling of exceptional data and 10% faulty parsing, all of which type safety would mitigate. That is 20 of the 40.

blocks.question: An attacker finds a buffer overflow in a C web server. On a Linux VM they get code execution as the unprivileged web server user. What changes if the same server runs as a unikernel without memory protections?
options: They get code execution with full control of the VM, including raw packet I/O, with no privilege escalation step needed
Nothing: the hypervisor stops the exploit before it runs
The exploit fails because unikernels have no shell to spawn
They can immediately read the memory of other VMs on the host
blocks.explain: With one address space and one privilege level, the application is the kernel. NCC Group showed arbitrary packet I/O right after compromise. The hypervisor still confines the attacker to that VM, so other tenants remain protected unless the hypervisor itself is broken.

blocks.question: A team ports a UDP service to a unikernel using the standard socket API on lwip, and it is slower than on a Linux VM. Which next step matches the evidence from the Unikraft key-value experiment?
options: Enable binary compatibility to use Linux's network stack
Add more vCPUs, since lwip scales linearly
Code the hot path against the uknetdev driver API in polling mode, bypassing the TCP/IP stack and sockets
Switch the allocator to buddy for better throughput
blocks.explain: lwip sockets gave 319 K/s; coding against uknetdev gave 6.3 M/s on one core. Binary compatibility does not bring Linux's network stack into the unikernel, and the evaluated images were single-core.

blocks.question: Which service is the weakest candidate for a unikernel?
options: A stateless HTTP API that must cold-start in milliseconds per request burst
A DNS server facing the internet where attack surface matters
A UDP packet processor that needs millions of packets per second per core
A CI build runner that shells out to compilers, git and test scripts in many child processes
blocks.explain: The build runner depends on fork, exec and many separate programs, which a single-process, single-address-space unikernel does not support. The other three match unikernel strengths: fast boot, small attack surface and low-level I/O specialization.

sources.label: Madhavapeddy et al., Unikernels: Library Operating Systems for the Cloud (ASPLOS 2013)
Kuenzer et al., Unikraft: Fast, Specialized Unikernels the Easy Way (EuroSys 2021)
